authored_explainer.title: Cereal Production Is 1.5x Higher Than in 1972
authored_explainer.hook: The 1970s warned of food shortages. Cereal output did the opposite.
says: In 1985, secondary-school progression was 77.8%; by 2017, 91.3%—1.2 times higher. Education access widened.
Cereal production rose from 1083.7 million metric tons in 1972 to 1644.1 million in 2024—1.5 times higher. Scarcity forecasts missed.
China leads farmland at 5.2 million square kilometers; United States 4.2, Australia 3.6, Brazil 2.4, Russia 2.2. Acreage isn't destiny.
authored_explainer.closing: More food came from productivity, not simply adding farmland.
authored_explainer.question: What changed food production most?

authored_explainer.title: Waste Energy Is 3.0x Higher Than in 1990
authored_explainer.hook: Since 1990, waste energy tripled—and methane rose with it.
says: In 1990, combustible renewables and waste supplied 10.2% of energy; by 2024, 30.1%—3.0 times higher. Waste became fuel.
Electricity access rose from 73.2% in 1998 to 91.9% in 2024—1.3 times higher. More people gained power.
Waste methane rose from 903.8 Mt CO2e in 1972 to 1,652 Mt CO2e in 2024—1.8 times higher. Recovery didn't erase emissions.
authored_explainer.closing: Using waste for energy still leaves an emissions problem to solve.
authored_explainer.question: Should waste energy count as clean?

authored_explainer.title: Population Growth Fell 54% Since 1972—But Population Rose
authored_explainer.hook: Population growth slowed sharply, but that never meant population decline.
says: Rural population fell from 63.1% in 1972 to 42.2% in 2025—down to 67% of its old share. Urbanization won.
The largest city's share moved from 18.2% in 1972 to 16.2% in 2025. Growth spread beyond the biggest city.
Population growth fell from 2% in 1972 to 0.91% in 2025—down to 46% of its old rate. Slower isn't smaller.
authored_explainer.closing: Slower growth still adds people, so cities must plan without assuming decline.
authored_explainer.question: How should cities plan for slower growth?
